title: Check Whether a Sensor Reading Is In Range (MISRA Essential Types)
statement:
Sensor readings only mean something inside a known range: outside it, the
value is noise, a fault, or a sensor that has not warmed up yet. This
function is the gate that decides which side of that line a reading falls
on.

This one is written to **MISRA C:2012**, like *Linear Interpolation Over a Calibration Table*. Nothing here runs a
static analyser over your submission -- the tests only check behaviour --
but the reference solution follows the rules below, and matching them is
the point of the exercise.

## Your function

```
bool in_range(int32_t value, int32_t low, int32_t high);
```

`low <= high` is guaranteed by every test. Return `true` if `value` is
inside `[low, high]` **inclusive of both ends**, `false` otherwise.

## The MISRA angle: essential types catch a real C bug

It is legal, ordinary-looking C to write the whole check as one chained
comparison:

```
return low <= value <= high;
```

This does not do what it looks like. Relational operators are
left-associative, so it parses as `(low <= value) <= high` -- the *result*
of the first comparison (`0` or `1`) is what actually gets compared to
`high`, not `value`. Concretely, with `low = 10`, `value = 5`,
`high = 20`: `10 <= 5` is `0`, and `0 <= 20` is `1` -- the function returns
`true` for a reading nowhere near the range, and it does this for
essentially any positive `high`, regardless of `value`.

MISRA's essential type model is exactly what rules this shape out: the
result of `low <= value` is essentially Boolean, and an essentially Boolean
value is not a valid operand of another relational operator against an
essentially signed one. A conforming static analyser rejects
`low <= value <= high` at the type level, before anyone has to notice the
logic is wrong at runtime. Writing the two comparisons out in full and
joining them with `&&` is not just clearer -- it is the only shape the
essential type model allows.

## Watch out

- **A fixed test is built around exactly the broken shape above.** A value
  below the range and a value above it are both queried; a chained
  comparison gets both wrong, in the same direction, for the same reason.
- Both ends of the range are inclusive: a `value` equal to `low` or `high`
  is in range, not out of it.
- `low == high` is a legal, single-point range -- test it as one rather than
  assuming a range always has room in it.

tests.name: the trap: a value below range a chained comparison would accept
tests.description: low <= value <= high parses as (10 <= 5) <= 20, which is 0 <= 20 -- true. 5 is not in [10, 20].

tests.name: the same trap on the other side of the range
tests.description: (10 <= 25) <= 20 is 1 <= 20 -- also wrongly true under the chained form. 25 is not in [10, 20] either.

tests.name: both ends of the range are inclusive
negative bounds work the same way as positive ones
